Given: The flow is a steady incompressible forced vortex flow . Key property of forced vortex: [latex]
v = \omega r
[/latex] Evaluation of statements: P: Shear stress is zero at all points in the flow. In a forced vortex, the fluid rotates like a rigid body. There is no relative motion between adjacent fluid layers, hence no velocity gradient in the radial direction. [latex]
\therefore \text{Shear stress} = 0
[/latex] Statement P is TRUE. Q: Vorticity is zero at all points in the flow. For a forced vortex, vorticity is given by [latex]
\text{Vorticity} = 2\omega
[/latex]

v = \omega r
[/latex]
Velocity increases linearly with radius. Statement R is TRUE. S: Total mechanical energy per unit mass is constant in the entire flow field. In a forced vortex, pressure and kinetic energy vary with radius, so total mechanical energy is not constant throughout the flow field (it is constant only along a streamline). Statement S is FALSE.

[latex]\begin{aligned} \delta &= 20mm=0.02m\\ q_G&= 80 MW/m^3\\ &= 80 \times 10^6 W/m^3\\ &= 80 \times 10^3 kW/m^3\\ T_{s=0} &= 160^{\circ}C\\ T_{s=\delta }&= 120^{\circ}C\\ k&=200 W/mK=0.20 kW/mK \end{aligned}[/latex]

Equation of one dimensional steady state heat transfer with heat generation
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d^2T}{dx^2}+\frac{q_G}{k}&=0\\ \frac{d^2T}{dx^2}+\frac{80 \times 10^3}{0.20}&=0\\ \frac{d^2T}{dx^2}+400 \times 10^3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
On integrating, we get
[latex] \frac{dT}{dx}+400 \times 10^3x=C_1[/latex]
Again integrating, we get
[latex] T+400 \times 10^3 \frac{x^2}{2}=C_1x+C_2[/latex]
[latex] T+200 \times 10^3 x^2=C_1x_2+C_2\;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
where [latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex] are constant of integration that can be determined from the boundary conditions
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{At}\;\; x&=0,\; T=160^{\circ}C \\ \therefore \;\; 160&=C_2 \\ C_2&=160 \\ \text{At}\;\; x &=\delta =0.02m, \; T=120^{\circ}C \\ \therefore \; &120+200 \times 10^3 \times (0.02)2& \\ &=C_1 \times 0.02+160 \\ 200&= 0.02C_1+160\\ 0.02C_1&= 40\\ C_1&=2000 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting the value of [latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex] in equation (i), we get
[latex] T+200 \times 10^3x^2=2000x+160[/latex]
[latex] T=2000x+160-200 \times 10^2x^2[/latex]

questions.question: A low carbon steel bar of 147 mm diameter with a length of 630 mm is being turned with uncoated carbide insert. The observed tool lives are 24 min and 12 min for cutting velocities of 90 m/min and     120 m/min respectively. The feed and depth of cut are 0.2 mm/rev and 2 mm respectively. Use the unmachined diameter to calculate the cutting velocity. When tool life is 20 min, the cutting velocity in m/min is
questions.explanation: Given, [latex]T_1=24 min, T_2 =12 min, V_1=90m/min, V_2=120m/min[/latex] We have to calculate velocity, when tool life is 20 minute. First of all we calculate the values of n, From the Taylor's tool life equation, [latex]VT^n=C[/latex] For case 1st and 2nd, we can write, [latex]\begin{aligned} V_1T_1^n &= V_2T_2^n\\ \left ( \frac{T_1}{T_2} \right )^n &= \frac{V_2}{V_1} \\ \left ( \frac{24}{12} \right )^n &=\frac{120}{90} \\ 2^n&= 1.33\\ n \log 2&=\log 1.33 \\ n \times 0.301 &=0.124 \\ n&= 0.412 \end{aligned}[/latex] For [latex]V_3[/latex], we can write from tool life equation, [latex]\begin{aligned} V_1T_1^n &= V_3T_3^n\\ 90 \times (24)^{0.412}&=V_3(20)^{0.412}\\ 333.34 &=V_3 \times 3.435\\ V_3 &=97\; m/min \end{aligned}[/latex]
